lead: A scene lives in world coordinates; the screen is a fixed grid of pixels. 2D viewing picks a rectangle of the scene, the window, and a rectangle of the screen, the viewport, then copies one onto the other with a scale and a shift. CAD drawings, chart axes, game minimaps and photo viewers all do this. The map is two multiplications and two additions, built from the transforms of 2.1 and 2.2.
prereq: You need: 2.1 for scaling and translation, and 2.2 for the 3×3 matrix form.

blocks.text: World coordinates are the units chosen for the scene: millimetres on a machine part, metres on a floor plan. They may be negative or very large. The display is a fixed grid of pixels counted from one screen corner.

items: Window: the rectangle of the world to show, fixed by xwmin, xwmax, ywmin, ywmax in world units.
Viewport: the rectangle of the display where it appears, fixed by xvmin, xvmax, yvmin, yvmax in device units, that is pixels.
Normalized coordinates: an optional middle system with both axes from 0 to 1, used when the final pixel size is not yet known, for example when a window may be resized.

blocks.text: The viewing pipeline carries every point from world to device coordinates: choose the window, map it onto the viewport, draw pixels. Parts outside the window are clipped away, covered in 2.6. Some syllabi call this map the 2D viewing transformation.
Two ideas do the whole job. Scale so the window's width becomes the viewport's width. Shift so the window's corner sits on the viewport's corner. The factors come from the two rectangles.
sx = (xvmax − xvmin) ÷ (xwmax − xwmin)   and   sy = (yvmax − yvmin) ÷ (ywmax − ywmin)
blocks.where: xwmin, xwmax are the left and right edges of the window in world units; xvmin, xvmax are the left and right edges of the viewport in device units; sx is how many device units one world unit covers across; sy does the same down the y axis.

blocks.text: Measure how far a point lies from the window's left edge: xw − xwmin. That distance becomes (xw − xwmin)·sx device units. Adding xvmin places it inside the viewport. The y direction works the same way.
xv = xvmin + (xw − xwmin)·sx    yv = yvmin + (yw − ywmin)·sy
blocks.where: (xw, yw) is the point in world coordinates; (xv, yv) is the same point in device coordinates; sx, sy are the scale factors above.

blocks.text: The map is one scale plus one shift, so it is affine: straight lines stay straight, parallel lines stay parallel, and ratios along a segment are kept. Joining two mapped endpoints therefore draws the correct line.
[xv, yv, 1]ᵀ = [[sx, 0, xvmin − xwmin·sx], [0, sy, yvmin − ywmin·sy], [0, 0, 1]] × [xw, yw, 1]ᵀ
blocks.where: the 3×3 array is the viewing matrix; the third row of zeros and one keeps it homogeneous, so it multiplies with the transforms of 2.3; the last column holds the shift.

blocks.text: The aspect ratio of a rectangle is its width divided by its height. When window and viewport have the same aspect ratio, sx and sy are equal and shapes keep their proportions.

When they differ, sx ≠ sy and the picture stretches along one axis: a circle becomes an ellipse, a square becomes a rectangle, text looks fat or thin. A window 10 wide and 5 high has aspect 2. In a 200 by 200 viewport, aspect 1, sx = 20 and sy = 40, so everything is drawn twice as tall as it should be.

items: Match the aspects: derive the viewport from the window's aspect.
Letterbox: keep the aspect and leave blank strips, as a phone does with an old film.
Allow the stretch only when deliberate, such as a chart made to fill a panel.

blocks.text: One exam question comes up again and again: what happens to a circle? It becomes an ellipse whose horizontal and vertical radii are in the ratio sx : sy.

figure.caption: The window is cut out of the world and placed on the viewport; the normalizing stage in grey is optional, and the final stage counts pixels.

spec.title: 2D viewing pipeline
spec.aria: A left-to-right chain from world coordinates through the chosen window, an optional normalizing stage and the viewport, ending in device coordinates.

examples.question: A drawing uses world coordinates. The window is (0, 0) to (10, 5) and the viewport is (0, 0) to (200, 100) in device units. (a) Find sx and sy and the device point for world point (5, 2.5). (b) The same window is shown in a viewport from (100, 60) to (300, 160). Find the device point for the same world point.
steps: Window width = 10 − 0 = 10 world units; height = 5 − 0 = 5 world units.
Viewport width = 200 − 0 = 200 device units; height = 100 − 0 = 100 device units.
(a) sx = 200 ÷ 10 = 20 device units per world unit. sy = 100 ÷ 5 = 20 device units per world unit.
Aspect check: window aspect = 10 ÷ 5 = 2; viewport aspect = 200 ÷ 100 = 2. Equal, so sx = sy and there is no stretch.
xv = 0 + (5 − 0)×20 = 100; yv = 0 + (2.5 − 0)×20 = 50. The centre of the window lands on the centre of the viewport.
(b) New viewport width = 300 − 100 = 200, height = 160 − 60 = 100. So sx = 20 and sy = 20, the same scales.
examples.answer: (a) sx = sy = 20 device units per world unit and (5, 2.5) maps to (100, 50) device units; (b) with the shifted viewport the same point maps to (200, 110) device units.
examples.check:
wxmin, wxmax, wymin, wymax = 0.0, 10.0, 0.0, 5.0
vxmin, vxmax, vymin, vymax = 0.0, 200.0, 0.0, 100.0
sx = (vxmax - vxmin) / (wxmax - wxmin)
sy = (vymax - vymin) / (wymax - wymin)
print(int(sx))
print(int(sy))
xw, yw = 5.0, 2.5
print(int(vxmin + (xw - wxmin) * sx))
print(int(vymin + (yw - wymin) * sy))
vxmin, vymin, vxmax, vymax = 100.0, 60.0, 300.0, 160.0
sx2 = (vxmax - vxmin) / (wxmax - wxmin)
sy2 = (vymax - vymin) / (wymax - wymin)
print(int(vxmin + (xw - wxmin) * sx2))
print(int(vymin + (yw - wymin) * sy2))

traps: Swapping window and viewport. The window lives in world units, the viewport in device units. Inverting the scale makes the picture explode or collapse.
Forgetting to subtract the window minimum. Using xv = xvmin + xw·sx instead of xvmin + (xw − xwmin)·sx shifts the picture by xwmin·sx whenever the window does not start at the origin.
Dropping xvmin or yvmin. The map then always lands in a viewport at the origin, so a viewport placed elsewhere puts the picture in the wrong place.
Using sx for both axes. sx and sy differ whenever the aspects differ, and using one for both stretches the scene along one direction.
The favourite question: sx ≠ sy turns a circle into an ellipse, with radii in the ratio sx : sy. Say ellipse, not circle, and give the ratio.

quiz.q: Define window and viewport, and state the coordinate system each one uses.
quiz.a: The window is the rectangle of the world to show, given by xwmin, xwmax, ywmin, ywmax in world coordinates. The viewport is the rectangle on the display where that content is drawn, given by xvmin, xvmax, yvmin, yvmax in device (pixel) coordinates.

quiz.q: Write the formulas for the two scale factors of a window-to-viewport mapping.
quiz.a: sx = (xvmax − xvmin) ÷ (xwmax − xwmin) and sy = (yvmax − yvmin) ÷ (ywmax − ywmin). sx is device units per world unit across; sy the same down.

quiz.q: Why does the mapping subtract xwmin before multiplying by sx, and add xvmin after?
quiz.a: Subtracting xwmin measures the point's distance from the window's left edge, so the scale acts on a distance, not an absolute coordinate. Adding xvmin starts that scaled distance at the viewport's left edge. Without the subtraction the shift xwmin·sx is wrong; without the addition the picture is pinned to the origin.

quiz.q: A window runs from (0, 0) to (8, 4). The viewport runs from (0, 0) to (160, 80). Find sx, sy and the device point for world point (6, 3).
The window is (−5, −5) to (5, 5) and the viewport is (0, 0) to (400, 400). Map world points (0, 0) and (5, 5).
A window 10 wide and 5 high is mapped into a viewport 200 wide and 200 high. What happens to a circle of radius 1 world unit at the centre of the window?
quiz.a: sx = 200 ÷ 10 = 20 and sy = 200 ÷ 5 = 40, so sx ≠ sy. The circle becomes an ellipse with horizontal radius 1×20 = 20 device units and vertical radius 1×40 = 40 device units. The aspect ratio is not preserved, so the drawing is stretched vertically.

quiz.q: Write the 3×3 viewing matrix for the window (0, 0) to (10, 5) and the viewport (0, 0) to (200, 100), and explain the last column.
quiz.a: sx = 20 and sy = 20, with xvmin − xwmin·sx = 0 − 0 = 0 and yvmin − ywmin·sy = 0. The matrix is [[20, 0, 0], [0, 20, 0], [0, 0, 1]]. The last column holds the shift, here zero because both rectangles start at the origin; for a viewport starting at (100, 60) the column would be (100, 60, 1).

beyond: Not for the exam. GPUs implement this map in hardware as the viewport transform, taking normalized device coordinates in the range −1 to 1 and producing window pixels; it is the same scale-and-shift, with the y axis often flipped. OpenGL's glViewport sets the viewport rectangle, and Vulkan allows a negative viewport height for that flip. Video players use the aspect-ratio rule as letterboxing and pillarboxing; games use it when a fixed 16:9 scene is shown on a phone with a different screen shape.
